blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: When precise details are uncertain, a coarser answer can retain useful information without guessing or abstaining. We investigate whether language models can learn this behavior through model-conditioned supervision derived from consistency across sampled responses and recognition of answers at different granularity levels. We evaluate LFM2.5-1.2B, Ministral~3~3B, Qwen3.5-9B, and Gemma~4~31B on temporal and geographic questions and three generalization datasets. In several in-domain settings, fine-tuning improves the balance of correctness and informativeness beyond coarsening base answers to the best fixed level. Across generalization datasets, all four models produce coarser answers more often at low than high base-model confidence. The three smaller models' answers are also preferred over base responses on held-out relations when correctness and granularity are considered jointly. These findings demonstrate learnable confidence-related granularity adaptation, with benefits varying by model.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Large language models (LLMs) encode substantial factual knowledge in their parameters ( Petroni et al., 2019 ; Roberts et al., 2020 ; Cohen et al., 2023 ) .
Nevertheless, they frequently generate plausible but factually incorrect
statements ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ) . One contributing factor is that common training and evaluation protocols reward guessing over acknowledging uncertainty, encouraging models to answer even when their knowledge is insufficient ( Kalai et al., 2025 ) . Such guesses are often highly specific: models may provide an unsupported day or city even when their predictions reliably support only a year or country ( Yona et al., 2024b ; Boggust et al., 2025 ) .

Existing approaches primarily adapt granularity by aggregating or abstracting
model outputs after generation ( Yona et al., 2024b ; Goren et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) .
Whether models can internalize this behavior and directly produce answers at an

answers at different granularity levels. These signals identify the finest
supported answer, with abstention targets when sampled responses lack
sufficient agreement. Fine-tuning teaches the model to produce these
answers directly.

blocks.en: 2 Background and Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 背景和有关工作

blocks.en:
The same entity or event can be described at multiple levels of abstraction,
from a specific instance to increasingly broad categories ( Rosch et al., 1976 ; Hobbs, 1985 ) . The appropriate level depends
on the available information, discourse context, and communicative purpose ( Mulkar-Mehta et al., 2011a ; Mulkar-Mehta et al., 2011b ) . Ellinger et al. (2026) introduce GranuScore , a
reference-free measure that estimates the granularity of arbitrary text
without requiring it to be mapped onto a predefined hierarchy. Our work
combines both perspectives: explicit hierarchies provide structured training
targets, while GranuScore enables evaluation beyond these hierarchies.

blocks.en:
Reliable generation requires models to recognize and communicate the
boundaries of their knowledge. Yona et al. (2026) argue that factuality
gains have primarily expanded these boundaries rather than models’ awareness
of them, while Park et al. (2026) provide evidence that models
possess useful metacognitive signals about what they know. Accordingly, prior
work argues that models should communicate uncertainty through linguistic
markers and develops methods to align these markers with model confidence ( Yona et al., 2024a ; Guo et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026b ) . These markers signal uncertainty but not its granularity: probably March 10, 1879 leaves unclear whether the uncertainty
concerns the day, month, or year.
We instead train models to adapt answer granularity accordingly, making explicit how precisely they can answer.

blocks.en:
Uncertainty about an answer is not directly observable from the generated text
and is therefore approximated using signals such as likelihood, sample
consistency, or self-assessment ( Kadavath et al., 2022 ; Kuhn et al., 2022 ; Manakul et al., 2023 ; Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2024 ; Cao et al., 2026 ) . These signals approximate the
model’s confidence, but confidence does not guarantee correctness: models may
confidently and consistently reproduce false associations learned during
training ( Cheang et al., 2026 ) . We therefore separate confidence from
factual correctness: sampled agreement determines the model-specific target
granularity, while external references determine correctness.

blocks.en:
Limited prior work has treated granularity as an alternative to binary
answer-or-abstain decisions. Yona et al. (2024b) introduce
multi-granularity question answering and DRAG , which aggregates
sampled predictions at inference time to return a coarser answer. Recent work applies
this principle to long-form generation by decomposing
responses into claims and replacing insufficiently supported claims with
coarser alternatives ( Goren et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) . We focus on
single-fact question answering, since hallucinations persist even in this
simplest setting ( Yona et al., 2026 ) , thereby isolating answer-level
granularity from the additional challenge of composing multiple claims.
While prior work adapts granularity through post-hoc procedures at inference
time, we use supervised fine-tuning to teach models to produce the supported
granularity directly.

blocks.en:
Our goal is not simply to make answers coarser, but to make
fine-grained knowledge reliably accessible when the model
supports it, while retaining coarser information when finer
details are uncertain.
Consistency and recognition provide complementary signals
for this: consistency identifies information the model
repeatedly generates, while recognition identifies supplied
answers it reliably distinguishes from distractors across the answer hierarchy.

The fixed-cap results illustrate the gap between supported
information and its expression.
For example, capping Ministral’s temporal predictions at
the year level raises accuracy from 38.36% to 74.53%,
showing that answers scored as incorrect often contain
correct information at a coarser level.

blocks.en:
Across all models and generalization datasets,
higher coarsening odds at lower base-model confidence
suggest that fine-tuning encourages confidence-related
granularity adaptation.
Adjusting for base-answer GranuScore and word count
provides further support, although these proxies may not
fully capture differences in starting granularity.
Complementary in-domain results show utility gains beyond
uniform coarsening in several settings, even against a cap selected to maximize test utility.
Unlike fixed caps, which require a predefined answer
hierarchy, confidence-related coarsening spans diverse
question types without a shared hierarchy.

Gemma illustrates that recovering more correct information

Our consensus threshold, fixed at 80% across models,

More fundamentally, consensus captures what the model
repeatedly produces, not whether it is true.

not a guarantee of consolidation.

Inference-time methods offer mixed benefits.
DRAG improves utility over Base in six of eight

construct training targets and generates one response

DRAG can also fail during aggregation: some inspected LFM
outputs repeated prompt content instead of combining
the sampled answers. IDK and granularity-aware prompting also require only one
response, but their gains are limited and vary across settings.
Their simplicity nevertheless motivates exploring combinations
of training and inference-time adaptation.

A natural next step is to broaden supervision beyond fixed

A stronger teacher could aggregate responses sampled from

However, without predefined hierarchies, granularity and
informativeness become harder to quantify, requiring
additional validation of the resulting supervision.

blocks.en: 6 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 6 结论

blocks.en:
Adapting answer granularity offers a way to retain useful
information when finer details are uncertain.
We introduced model-conditioned supervision based on
consistency and recognition to consolidate demonstrated
knowledge into generation.
Fine-tuning improves the balance between correctness and
informativeness in several settings and produces
confidence-related granularity changes.

知识进入世代。

在若干场合提供信息并制作
与信心相关的颗粒性变化。

blocks.en:
These results establish granularity adaptation as a
learnable answering behavior and motivate training models
not only on what to answer, but also on how precisely
to express it.

可学习的应答行为和激励培训模式

blocks.en: Limitations
blocks.zh: 限制

blocks.en:
Geographic normalization assumes that a model naming
a location also knows the regions or country containing it.
Wikidata completion can therefore introduce information
into consensus targets and rewritten answers.
Recognition similarly filters externally supplied answers,
but preference over distractors does not establish that
the model could generate them unaided.
Thus, these external inputs may contribute to the gains alongside
the consolidation of existing knowledge.

地理正常化假定一个模型命名

因此,Wikidata完成可以引入信息
并重写答案。
同样识别外部提供的答案,
但优于分散注意力者并不能证明
模型可以无助地生成它们。
因此,这些外部投入可以促进取得这些成果,同时,
巩固现有知识。

blocks.en:
Extraction, normalization, and automatic judgments remain
imperfect despite auditing and corrections.
Fine-tuned responses tend to be shorter and may be
structurally simpler, potentially making them easier to
extract and normalize. Processing errors could therefore differ across methods. Nevertheless, temporal and open-ended evaluations strengthen the evidence for granularity adaptation without relying on geographic extraction and normalization.
blocks.zh:
采掘、正常化和自动判决仍然存在
尽管进行了审计和纠正,但并不完美。
微调后的反应往往较短,而且可能
结构简单,有可能使它们更容易
提取和正常化。 因此,处理错误可能因方法而异。 然而,时间性和开放式的评价加强了颗粒性适应的证据,而不依赖于地理提取和正常化。

blocks.en:
We treat Wikidata’s recorded precision as the finest verifiable granularity.
A correct finer answer may therefore be scored as incorrect
if the additional detail is known but missing from Wikidata.
Its extensive coverage should limit this issue, although
we have not independently verified reference completeness.
Additionally, we do not evaluate alternatives as sets of possibilities: conflicting alternatives such as “either A or B” are non-evaluable, even when they convey useful partial information.

我们把Wikidata记录的精度视为最好的可核查颗粒。
因此,正确的更细的答案可能会被评为不正确
如果额外细节已知, 但从 Wikidata 中缺失。
其广泛范围应限制这一问题,尽管
我们没有独立核实参考材料的完整性。
此外,我们不评价替代方法作为各种可能性:相互冲突的替代方法,例如“A或B”是不可评价的,即使它们传递有用的部分信息。

blocks.en:
Our Generalization evaluation uses only the first sentence
to reduce the influence of verbosity on granularity judgments.
This may omit relevant information, qualifications, or errors
appearing later in the response.

减少动词对颗粒性判断的影响。
这可能省略有关信息、资格或错误

Open-ended granularity remains difficult to measure,

agreement with the final labels but remain imperfect

Using both provides a robustness check, without removing
uncertainty in these judgments.

Utility assumes a uniform prior and a fixed error penalty,
overlooking contextual differences in information value. Besides that, experiments cover English factual questions and one main
training seed per model, leaving robustness across seeds,
languages, and longer-form responses unestablished.

Fixed caps preserve base-model abstentions, whereas

blocks.en: Ethical considerations
blocks.zh: 道德考虑

blocks.en:
This work aims to reduce unsupported specificity by encouraging language models to answer at a granularity supported by their knowledge or to abstain. The method does not guarantee factual correctness, and its model-specific targets may inherit errors and biases from the underlying models and datasets. In particular, models may provide coarser answers or abstain more frequently for underrepresented entities and regions. These limitations should be
considered when applying the method in high-stakes settings. Our experiments use publicly available models and factual resources.

这项工作的目的是通过鼓励语言模型在知识所支持的颗粒化状态下回答或弃权来降低不支持的特异性. 该方法不能保证事实正确性,其模式特定目标可能继承基础模型和数据集的错误和偏差. 特别是,模型可能为任职人数不足的实体和区域提供较简洁的答案或更经常地弃权。 这些限制应当是:

blocks.en: C.1 Temporal Parsing
blocks.zh: C.1 时间分析

blocks.en:
A deterministic, rule-based parser identifies temporal
expressions and their granularity, including dates, seasons,
years, decades, centuries, and early/mid/late modifiers.
Event cues such as “born” and “died” distinguish dates
relevant to the requested relation.
Coarser representations follow directly from the parsed
value: for example, 14 March 1879 implies March 1879,
spring 1879, 1879, the 1870s, and the nineteenth century,
without external factual lookup. When several expressions refer to the requested event, the parser retains the finest compatible value. Conflicting alternatives and malformed or incomplete expressions are flagged as non-evaluable.

blocks.en: C.2 Geographic Parsing

blocks.en:
Geographic parsing separates extraction from normalization.
The extractor, a fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B model, identifies
locations stated for the requested birth or death event,
while the normalizer resolves their identities and geographic
hierarchies using Wikidata.

blocks.en:
Geographic information can be distributed across clauses
or sentences, making rule-based extraction difficult. For example, “She was born in North Rhine-Westphalia.
More precisely, she was born at her family home in Munich”
contains three components: North Rhine-Westphalia , her family home , and Munich .
The extractor collects all three because they describe
the requested birth event.
The normalizer can then complete geographic hierarchies,
such as Munich–Bavaria–Germany–Europe.
More specific places, such as her family home , and subcity units are retained where available.

blocks.en:
A response is fully normalized when its extracted
components can be resolved into one consistent geographic
hierarchy.
It is partially normalized when some components remain
unresolved or cannot be combined into a consistent hierarchy.
In the example above, Munich belongs to Bavaria rather than
North Rhine-Westphalia, so the components conflict.
Both locations nevertheless belong to Germany.
The normalizer therefore retains Germany and Europe as
the within-answer consensus value .
We provide details on extraction, entity search, candidate
selection, and hierarchy completion in Appendix G .

or subcity levels. We filter region ancestors using the same rules as
prediction normalization, rather than treating every
administrative ancestor as a region.

Suitable temporal answers must contain exactly one valid
temporal expression in the entire response and no extracted
location.
The expression must refer to the requested birth or death event.
This restriction avoids adapting one temporal claim while
leaving others unchanged.
For example, an answer containing both a death date and
a reign period is excluded, since replacing only the death
date would leave the other temporal information uncontrolled. We rewrite the responses using rule-based substitution,
replacing the temporal expression with the common value
while retaining the text through the end of its sentence
and discarding subsequent text.

The rewriter expresses the common value while preserving

For each answer level, we select 20 distractors from other
questions with the same relation and normalized granularity level.
We exclude answers that occur together in a hierarchy, since
they may be valid abstractions of one another. We also exclude pairs when at least half the distinct words
in either answer occur in the other, or when at least 80%
of either answer’s distinct character trigrams occur in the other.
These rules apply both between the candidate and its distractors
and among the distractors themselves.
Levels with fewer than 20 eligible distractors are treated
as unsupported.

We then score the supplied answer and each distractor
independently as assistant continuations, using the base

To reduce dependence on question wording, we repeat this
comparison for the original question and two relation-specific
paraphrases.
A level passes only if its supplied answer scores strictly

Adding word count improves agreement with human judgments,
suggesting that length provides a complementary signal to GranuScore .
Additional words can express finer-grained distinctions,
but can also increase sentence specificity without changing
granularity.
Sentence specificity concerns the amount of descriptive
information conveyed, whereas granularity concerns the level
of referential expressions within a semantic hierarchy ( Ellinger et al., 2026 ) .

without changing the granularity of its referents.
